cards.front: Define abstraction in computational thinking and say why it matters.
cards.back: Removing detail that is not needed for the task at hand so that only what matters remains. It makes a problem tractable, and a model built this way can be reused for other purposes.

keyPoints.text: keeping only what matters for the task
makes the problem simpler or the model reusable

cards.explanation: The London Underground map is the classic example: it distorts geography deliberately because only the connections matter.

cards.back: Breaking a complex problem or system into smaller, more manageable parts that can be understood, solved or built separately, then combining the results.

keyPoints.text: parts are easier to handle separately

mcq.correct: Breaking a complex problem or system into smaller, more manageable parts that can be understood, solved or built separately, then combining the results.
distractors: Removing unnecessary detail from a problem
Reusing a solution from a similar problem
Writing the steps of a solution in order

cards.explanation: Those three options are abstraction, pattern recognition and algorithmic thinking: the four skills are easy to confuse in an exam.

cards.back: Working out a clear, ordered sequence of steps that solves a problem, including the decisions and repetitions needed, so precisely that it could be carried out by a machine or by someone else.

keyPoints.text: precise enough to be carried out mechanically

cards.explanation: A recipe is algorithmic; 'cook something nice' is not, because the steps are not definite.

cards.front: What is pattern recognition, and how does it help solve a problem?
cards.back: Spotting similarities or trends within a problem, or between it and problems already solved, so that a known technique or an existing solution can be reused instead of starting from scratch.

keyPoints.text: within the problem or between problems
lets an existing approach be reused

cards.explanation: Recognising that a task is really a search or a sort lets you reuse a known algorithm and its known complexity.

cards.front: A train timetable shows only the departure and arrival time at each station, not the colour of the train or the driver's name. Which thinking skill is this, and why is it useful?
cards.back: Abstraction. Only the details needed for the task are kept, which makes the model simpler to reason about and lets the same timetable serve other purposes, such as planning a journey or checking a connection.

keyPoints.text: the model is simpler or reusable

cards.explanation: The test for abstraction is always the same: does the missing detail change any answer the model is used for? Here it does not.

cards.front: Decompose the problem 'design a vending machine' into four sub-problems.
cards.back: For example: taking and validating payment, selecting and dispensing the item, managing and restocking stock, and handling faults and giving change.
cards.explanation: Decomposition is judged on whether the parts are genuinely separable and together cover the whole problem. The four listed have clean interfaces between them - payment does not need to know how the motor turns - which is the test of a good split. A decomposition where every part needs to know about every other part has not actually reduced the difficulty.

cards.front: Give two examples of abstraction in everyday computing, and say what is hidden in each.
cards.back: A file system hides the physical sectors and blocks on the disk behind names and folders; a function interface hides its implementation behind a name, parameters and a return type.

keyPoints.text: a file system hides physical sectors
synonyms: names and folders hide the hardware
the interface hides how it works

mcq.correct: A file system hides sectors; a function interface hides its implementation
distractors: A file system hides files; a function hides its parameters
Abstraction only applies to hardware, not to programs
Abstraction means writing shorter programs

cards.explanation: In both cases the user works with a simplified model and cannot get the details wrong, because the details are not exposed. Abstraction is what makes layers stackable: a program can use a file without knowing about the disk, and the disk driver can change without the program changing. Confusing abstraction with merely shortening code is a common misreading.

cards.front: What three properties must a set of instructions have to count as an algorithm?
cards.back: It must be unambiguous, finite - it must terminate - and it must have well defined inputs and outputs.

mcq.correct: Unambiguous, finite, with defined inputs and outputs
distractors: Fast, memory efficient and correct
Written in pseudocode, tested and documented
Recursive, iterative and terminating

cards.explanation: An unambiguous procedure that never stops - such as repeatedly adding 1 to a counter - is a process but not an algorithm. Termination is the property most often forgotten, and it is the one that separates a specification from a recipe. Efficiency and correctness are desirable properties of a good algorithm but not part of the definition.

cards.front: How does pattern recognition help when designing a program to check whether a string is a palindrome?
cards.back: Recognising that a palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards means the same comparison - first against last, second against second-last - repeats with changing indices, so a single loop with two moving pointers solves it.

synonyms: the pattern has a changing index

keyPoints.text: so a loop with two pointers does the whole job

mcq.correct: The comparison repeats with changing indices, so one loop suffices
distractors: Palindromes are always even in length, so the string can be halved
Every character must be compared with every other character
The string must be sorted before it can be checked

cards.explanation: Spotting the repeated structure converts what looks like $\frac{n^2}{2}$ comparisons into $n/2$ of them. This is the practical value of pattern recognition: it does not just make a program tidier, it usually changes its complexity. Comparing every character with every other would be correct but quadratic, and sorting would destroy the order that defines a palindrome.

cards.front: State four criteria you would use to evaluate two competing algorithms for the same task.
cards.back: Time complexity, space complexity, correctness across all inputs including edge cases, and ease of implementation or maintenance.

synonyms: how hard it is to write

mcq.correct: Time, space, correctness on edge cases, and maintainability
distractors: Time only
Programming language, file size, comments and author
Speed of coding, speed of running, cost and popularity

cards.explanation: Evaluating on time alone misses that a fast algorithm using $O(n^2)$ memory may not run at all on the available hardware, and misses that an algorithm failing on an empty list is simply wrong. The relative weight of the criteria depends on context: an embedded device weighs memory heavily, while a one-off script weighs implementation effort.

cards.front: A program must reject a password unless it is at least 8 characters long AND contains a digit OR contains a capital letter. Write the condition and say what a password of 5 characters with a digit does.
cards.back: `length >= 8 AND (hasDigit OR hasCapital)`. A 5-character password with a digit is rejected, because the length condition fails.

synonyms: AND binds the length test to the rest

keyPoints.text: a 5-character password with a digit is rejected

mcq.correct: Rejected: `length >= 8 AND (hasDigit OR hasCapital)` fails on length
distractors: Accepted: it contains a digit
Rejected only if it has no capital as well
Accepted: 5 is close enough to 8

cards.explanation: Without brackets, `length >= 8 AND hasDigit OR hasCapital` would accept a 3-character password containing a capital, since OR has the lower precedence. Bracketing the OR is what makes the length requirement unconditional. Writing the condition out and testing one boundary case against it is the fastest way to catch this class of error.

cards.front: How does generalisation differ from abstraction?
cards.back: Generalisation takes several specific cases and produces one rule covering them all; abstraction removes detail that is not needed for the task at hand.

keyPoints.text: generalisation combines specific cases into one rule

mcq.correct: Generalisation combines cases into one rule; abstraction removes irrelevant detail
distractors: They mean the same thing
Generalisation removes detail; abstraction combines cases
Generalisation applies to data and abstraction only to hardware

cards.explanation: Seeing that squares, rectangles and triangles all have an area, and writing one routine that takes a shape, is generalisation. Drawing a map that omits the colour of the buildings is abstraction. The two often happen together, which is why they are confused - but a routine can be fully general while still exposing every unnecessary detail.
